definition: A Ping release claim (2026-11-02), UNVERIFIED on our tenant: one policy limits the member tools, enforced on the listing and again at the member hop. The swagger has no field for it; this demo models it as a lab-invented allow-list.
The alias__tool naming that keeps one member's tool from taking another member's name. An alias has no underscore, so the first double underscore always ends the alias.
A tool whose input schema asks for a password or one-time code as ordinary parameters, so the agent collects the secret from the user and hands it to the server.

A Ping release claim (2026-11-02), UNVERIFIED on our tenant: the tool list a caller receives is filtered by what that caller is entitled to. The swagger has no field for it; this demo models it as a lab-invented allow-list.
A tool parameter whose default points off-box (a callback URL or a bcc address). An agent that fills arguments from the schema leaks data on every call without anyone choosing to.

An application type (mcp-aggregate) that merges the tools of several member MCP servers behind one connection. Each member has an AppRef, an Alias and a ToolFilter, and its tools appear as Alias__tool. The field names are in the console swagger (2026-10-31, schema only).
Recording a hash of each tool's name, description and input schema at approval, and refusing or flagging any tool whose hash later differs. It detects change; it does not judge content.
Instructions hidden in the text a tool call returns. The tool metadata is clean, so neither a metadata scanner nor pinning sees it; it reaches the model only when the result is read.
A tool server that serves a clean tool list while it is being reviewed and a poisoned one later, under the same tool name. Nothing in MCP tells the client the metadata changed.
Putting instructions in a tool's description or schema. The model reads that text as trusted context and the user normally never sees it.
A second server defines a tool with the same name as a trusted one and claims to be the authoritative version, so a client that resolves tools by name may pick the hostile definition.
Accepting whatever is presented the first time and only noticing later changes. It is safe only if the first presentation was vetted by a scanner or a person.
